newsitem.title: TUNISIA: Libya sentences eight to death as CIA-linked spies.
newsitem.headline: Libya sentences eight to death as CIA-linked spies.

text.p: Libya's top military court has sentenced six senior officers and two civilians to death for spying, using equipment supplied by the U.S. Central Intelligence Agency, Libyan state-run radio said on Thursday.
"The sentence was issued by the Supreme Military Court on Wednesday," one official contacted by telephone said. He would not elaborate.
The radio, monitored in Tunis, said the men were convicted of belonging to "a banned organisation linked to agents of foreign governments" and of passing defence secrets to foreign states.
It did not name the governments but said the convicted men used CIA-supplied equipment and implied they were spying for the United States.
In Washington, U.S. officials dismissed the trial as a propaganda ploy.
"This is not a new case and the proceedings have a show trial flavor," one official said. "They look like a propaganda ploy for internal consumption." The CIA declined comment.
"The report is the first public admission of opposition within the military to the rule of Colonel Muammar Gaddafi," a Tripoli-based diplomat said.
Libya's state-run television on Wednesday night broadcast footage of the trial room in an unidentified place.

"You mobilised yourselves as spies against your country and allowed the enemies to get hold of military, economic and security capabilities by using sophisticated equipment supplied by the CIA," the television showed an unnamed prosecutor dressed in civilian clothes as telling the men.

"Have you forgotten or are you just playing down what those who recruited you as spies, have done to us? They killed our children, tore our bodies apart, raided our families as they were sleeping late in the night," he said, in an apparent reference to the U.S. bombing of Tripoli and Benghazi in 1986.

Six of those found guilty would be executed by firing squad and two by hanging, the radio said. It did not say when. In theory, only Gaddafi can decide to carry on or not the execution, but the prosecutor seemed to exclude any clemency.
"You only can demand that the sentence be implemented on you if you really want to show your repentance," he told them.
Six other officers and two civilians were acquitted, showing that the "revolution is able to be clement when there is lack of evidence", the radio said.

"The Supreme Military Court...has passed its sentences against the agent-spies who sold their honour, dignity and homeland to their enemies and supplied agents of foreign governments with information relating to the country's defence secrets, for espionage purposes, by exploiting their membership of the Libyan army," it said.

U.S. military aircraft bombed targets in Tripoli and Benghazi on April 15, 1986. Ten days earlier a bomb had exploded in a West Berlin disco, killing a U.S. soldier and a Turkish woman. The United States accused Libya of instigating that incident and other attacks against U.S. targets in the Middle East and Europe.
Libyan television showed pictures of the courtroom where about 12 of the accused could be seen seated in a large cage, and attendees were over 100.
The heads of the accused were shaved and they appeared to be wearing prison uniforms.

Those sentenced to death were named as Colonel Muftah Muhammad Gharoum, Staff Colonel Mustafa Abu al-Qasim Massud, Flight Lieutenant-Colonel Saad Salah Faraj, Major Khalil Salim Muhammad, Major Ramadan al-Ihumi Muhammad Ali and Major Mustafa Hubayl al-Fudhil.
Two civilians, named as Misbah Saad Musbah and Sulayman Ghayth Muftah, were sentenced to death by hanging.
